documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1 — Phosphoric Acid
problems.statement:
The elemental phosphorus is present in the nature as phosphate in a complex mineral apatite. This mineral contains, in addition to phosphate, silica and the following ions: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{SiO_3^{2-}}$, and $\mathrm{F^-}$.

Let us assume that this mineral is a mixture of tricalcium phosphate, $\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}$, calcium sulphate, calcium fluoride, calcium carbonate and silica.

For uses as fertilizer the calcium bis(dihydrogenphosphate), $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$, which is soluble in water, has been prepared. For this purpose, apatite is treated with a mixture of phosphoric and sulphuric acid. At the same time this operation eliminates the majority of impurities.

The elemental analysis of an apatite gave the following results in which, except of fluorine, the elemental composition is expressed as if the elements were in the form of oxides:

| Component | $\mathrm{CaO}$ | $\mathrm{P_2O_5}$ | $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ | F | $\mathrm{SO_3}$ | $\mathrm{CO_2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| % by mass | 47.3 | 28.4 | 3.4 | 3.4 | 3.5 | 6.1 |

**Operation 1.** A sample of $m_0$ of this mineral is treated with $50.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of a solution containing $0.500\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ phosphoric and $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ sulphuric acids. The mixture is completely dehydrated by heating up to about $70\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$ avoiding temperature rising above $90\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$. This operation is carried out under the hood since toxic gaseous substances are emitted. The dry residue is ground and weighed; $m_1$ is the mass of the residue obtained. In these conditions only dihydrogenphosphate, $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$, is formed while silica and silicate do not react.

**Operation 2.** $1.00\ \mathrm{g}$ of this residue is treated with $50.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of water at $40\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$, then filtered, dried and weighed. The mass of the residue obtained is $m_2$. This new residue is mainly containing gypsum, $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O}$, whose solubility can be considered as constant between $20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and is equal to $2.3\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$.

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement: Write the balanced equations for the reactions that are involved.

From what mass of apatite should one start if all the reactions are stoichiometric?

Starting with $m_0$ of obtained apatite, $m_1=5.49\ \mathrm{g}$ of residue are obtained.
What mass should theoretically be obtained?

This result is due to the presence of products that are not expected to be found in the residue. Give two of them that under these experimental conditions can plausibly account for the data.

Traditionally, in industry the analysis and the yield are expressed as percentage of oxide. The phosphorous content is expressed as if it were $\mathrm{P_2O_5}$.

If $n_2$ is the amount of a soluble product obtained, $n_1$ the amount of a substance added as acid, $n_0$ the amount of apatite added, the yield is:

$$
r_{\mathrm{exp}}=\frac{n_2}{n_1+n_0}\,100.
$$

$m_2=0.144\ \mathrm{g}$ of residue is obtained on the filter.
Calculate $r_{\mathrm{exp}}$.

The experimental yield is over 100%. Calculate a value of $r$ nearer to the real yield.

Relative atomic masses: P: 31; Ca: 40; O: 16; H: 1; F: 19; C: 12; Si: 28; S: 32.

Values of $pK$:

| Acid/base pair | $pK$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\mathrm{HSO_4^-}/\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ | 2 |
| $\mathrm{HF}/\mathrm{F^-}$ | 3 |
| $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}/\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ | 2 |
| $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}/\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ | 7 |
| $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}/\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ | 12 |

sections.statement:
The following equations are transcribed literally from the collection:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}+4\mathrm{H_3PO_4}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}+2\mathrm{HF},\\
\mathrm{CaCO_3}+2\mathrm{H_3PO_4}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}+\mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow+\mathrm{H_2O},\\
\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}+2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}+4\mathrm{H_2O}&\longrightarrow2\mathrm{CaSO_4}+2\mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2},\\
\mathrm{CaF_2}+\mathrm{H_2SO_4}+2\mathrm{H_2O}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O}+2\mathrm{HF}\uparrow,\\
\mathrm{CaCO_3}+\mathrm{H_2SO_4}+\mathrm{H_2O}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O}+\mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow.
\end{aligned}
$$

$1\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite contains:

$$
\frac{0.284}{142}=2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ of\ Ca_3(PO_4)_2},
$$

$$
\frac{0.034}{2+19}=0.89\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ of\ CaF_2},
\qquad
\frac{0.061}{44}=1.39\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ of\ CaCO_3},
$$

$$
\frac{0.035}{80}=0.44\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ of\ CaSO_4},
$$

$$
\frac{0.473}{56}-\frac{3\times0.284}{142}
-\frac{0.034}{38}-\frac{0.061}{44}-\frac{0.035}{80}
=2.72\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ CaO\ that\ remain}.
$$

The amount of $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ needed to react with $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite is equal to:

$$
n(\mathrm{H_3PO_4})
=4n(\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2})+2n(\mathrm{CaF_2})+2n(\mathrm{CaCO_3})
=12.56\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

$50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the acid contains $25\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$, therefore $25/12.56=1.99\ \mathrm{g}$ apatite is needed to neutralize the $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ present.

The amount of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ needed to react with $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite can be calculated in the same way:

$$
n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4})
=2n(\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2})+n(\mathrm{CaF_2})+n(\mathrm{CaCO_3})
=6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

$50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the acid contains $5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of sulphuric acid. Therefore $5/6.28=0.80\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite is needed to neutralize the $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. The total amount of apatite is $m_0=1.99+0.80=2.79\ \mathrm{g}$.

Formation of $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$:

$1.99\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite needed to neutralize the $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ contains $1.9\times2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}$, thus $3\times2\times2\times10^{-3}=1.2\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of dihydrogen phosphate is being formed.

From $\mathrm{CaF_2}$, $1.99\times0.89=1.80\ \mathrm{mol}$ and from $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, $1.99\times1.39=2.77\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$ are formed.

$0.8\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite that reacts with $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the sulphuric acid yields $2\times0.8\times10^{-3}=1.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$.

The printed dimensional equality is:

$$
m(\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2})=18.07\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}=4.230\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

Formation of gypsum:

$$
n(\mathrm{CaSO_4})=n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4})=5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}
\ \widehat{=}\ 0.86\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

The amount of $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ that was already present in $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of apatite and yielded gypsum is $0.434\times10^{-3}\times172=0.075\ \mathrm{g}$. There remain also $0.034\ \mathrm{g}$ of silica, and thus the theoretical mass of the residue should be:

$$
m_{\mathrm{th}}=4.230+0.86+(0.0753+0.034)\times2.79=5.39\ \mathrm{g}.
$$
The difference of $0.1\ \mathrm{g}$ may be due to water and unreacted $\mathrm{CaF_2}$ in the residue.

The second reaction is intended to dissolve $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$, while all the other products remain on the filter.

According to the yielded residue of $0.144\ \mathrm{g}$, $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of residue contains $1-0.144=0.856\ \mathrm{g}$ of soluble product. If it were all $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$ it would correspond to $0.856/234=3.66\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$. For $5.49\ \mathrm{g}$ of residue it is $0.0201\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of soluble product ($n_2$). The amount of acid used is $0.500/20=0.025\ \mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ (equals $0.0125\ \mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{P_2O_5}$) and $0.005\ \mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. The amount of $\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}$ in $2.79\ \mathrm{g}$ apatite is $0.00558\ \mathrm{mol}$ (equals $0.00558\ \mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{P_2O_5}$). So:

$$
r_{\mathrm{exp}}=100\times\frac{0.0201}{0.0125+0.00558}=111\%.
$$

Since $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ water dissolve $0.115\ \mathrm{g}$ of gypsum, the real quantity of $\mathrm{Ca(H_2PO_4)_2}$ is $0.856-0.115=0.741\ \mathrm{mol}$, so that the real yield gives:

$$
r_{\mathrm{exp}}=100\times\frac{0.0174}{0.0125+0.00558}=96\%.
$$

The theoretical value for $r_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is:

$$
r_{\mathrm{exp}}
=100\times\frac{4.23/234}{0.0125+0.00558}=100\%,
$$

so this calculation makes sense.

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The first printed reaction produces HF with no F on its left. The third prints water separately on both sides. The $\mathrm{CaF_2}$ denominator $2+19$, factors $1.99/1.9$, products $1.80\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $2.77\ \mathrm{mol}$, dimensional equality for $m$, $n_2$ exponent, $0.741\ \mathrm{mol}$ and native placement of 96% under 1.5 versus 100% under 1.6 are all retained without repair. The residual $\mathrm{CaO}$ exponent is clearly **negative four**; the earlier reader-note allegation of positive four was superseded by native-image zoom.

problems.title: Problem 2 — Ionic Solutions: Aqueous Solutions of Copper Salts

sections.title: Acidity of the hydrated copper(II) ion and precipitation of the hydroxide
sections.statement: Consider a $1.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solution of copper(II) nitrate. The pH of this solution is 4.65.

parts.statement: Give the equation for the formation of the conjugate base of the hydrated $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion.

Calculate the $pK_a$ of the corresponding acid-base pair.

The solubility product of copper(II) hydroxide is $K_{\mathrm{sp}}=1\times10^{-20}$.

At what pH value hydroxide $\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2}$ precipitates from the solution under consideration? Justify your calculation showing that the conjugate base of this hydrated $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion is present in negligible quantity.

sections.title: Disproportionation of copper(I) ions
sections.statement:
The $\mathrm{Cu^+}$ ion is involved in two redox couples:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Couple 1:}\quad\mathrm{Cu^+}+\mathrm{e^-}&\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cu},
&E_1^0&=+0.52\ \mathrm{V},\\
\text{Couple 2:}\quad\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}+\mathrm{e^-}&\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cu^+},
&E_2^0&=+0.16\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$

parts.statement: Write down the equation for the disproportionation of copper(I) ions and calculate the corresponding equilibrium constant.
Calculate the composition of the solution (in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) obtained on dissolving $1.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of copper(I) in $1.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ of water.

Apart from $\mathrm{Cu^+}$ ions, name two chemical species which also disproportionate in aqueous solution; write down the equations and describe the experimental conditions under which disproportionation is observed.

Consider the stability of copper(I) oxide, $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$, in contact with a $1.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solution of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ions. The solubility product of copper(I) oxide is $K_{\mathrm{sp}}=[\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]=1\times10^{-15}$.
Calculate the pH value at which $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ becomes stable. Quote a simple experiment allowing the observation of the precipitation of $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$.

sections.title: Complex formation involving copper(I) and copper(II) ions

parts.statement:
The dissociation constant of the complex ion $\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}$ is $K_D=1\times10^{-11}$. Calculate the standard electrode potential of the couple:

$$
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+\mathrm{e^-}
\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cu}+2\mathrm{NH_3}.
$$

Deduce from it the standard electrode potential of the couple:

$$
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}+\mathrm{e^-}
\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+2\mathrm{NH_3}.
$$

Does the disproportionation of the cation $\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}$ take place?

sections.statement:
$$
\mathrm{[Cu(H_2O)_4]^{2+}}+\mathrm{H_2O}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{H_3O^+}+\mathrm{[Cu(OH)(H_2O)_3]^+}.
$$

$$
2\mathrm{Cu^+}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}+\mathrm{Cu},
\qquad
K=\frac{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^+}]^2}.
$$

$$
0.52-0.16=0.059\log K\quad\text{(Nernst equation)}
\ \Longrightarrow\ K=1\times10^6.
$$

At equilibrium:

$$
[\mathrm{Cu^+}]+2[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]=1\times10^{-2},
\qquad
[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]=1\times10^6[\mathrm{Cu^+}],
$$

so that the following equation is obtained:

$$
2\times10^6[\mathrm{Cu^+}]^2+[\mathrm{Cu^+}]-1\times10^{-2}=0,
$$

with the solution $[\mathrm{Cu^+}]=7.07\times10^{-5}$ and $[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]=4.96\times10^{-3}$.

Other disproportionation reactions:

$$
2\mathrm{H_2O_2}\longrightarrow2\mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{O_2}
\quad\text{(catalyzed by }\mathrm{KMnO_4},\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\text{ etc.)},
$$

$$
\mathrm{Cl_2}+\mathrm{OH^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{ClO^-}
\quad\text{(basic conditions)}.
$$

$$
\mathrm{Cu_2O}+2\mathrm{H_3O^+}+2\mathrm{e^-}
\longrightarrow2\mathrm{Cu}+3\mathrm{H_2O},
\qquad
[\mathrm{Cu^+}]=\frac{1\times10^{-15}}{[\mathrm{OH^-}]}.
$$

$$
E_1=0.52+\frac{0.059}{2}\log\left([\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^2\right)
=0.49-0.0885\,\mathrm{pH}.
$$

$$
2\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}+3\mathrm{H_2O}+2\mathrm{e^-}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu_2O}+2\mathrm{H_3O^+},
$$

$$
E_2=0.16+\frac{0.059}{2}
\log\frac{1\times10^{-4}}{[\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^2}
=0.07+0.0885\,\mathrm{pH}.
$$

$\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ is stable when $E_2>E_1$, i.e. $0.42<0.177\,\mathrm{pH}$, or $\mathrm{pH}>2.4$.

$\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ can be obtained by the reduction of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ in acid or basic media, e.g. by Fehling's solution or reducing sugars.

$$
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Cu^+}+2\mathrm{NH_3},
\qquad
K_D=\frac{[\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}]}
=1\times10^{-11}.
$$

Knowing $E^0(\mathrm{Cu^+/Cu})=0.52\ \mathrm{V}$, the printed $E^0(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+/Cu^+})$ becomes:

$$
E_{\mathrm{f1}}=0.52-0.06\,pK_D=-0.14\ \mathrm{V}.
$$

The standard emf of a $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}$ cell is thus:

$$
E^0=\frac{0.5+0.16}{2}=0.33\ \mathrm{V},
\qquad E_3^0=0.33-0.03\,pK_2.
$$

Thereout:

$$
pK_2=\frac{0.33-E_3^0}{0.03}
=\frac{0.33-(-0.02)}{0.03}=12.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}+2\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu}+4\mathrm{NH_3},
&E^0&=-0.02\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu}+2\mathrm{NH_3},
&E^0&=-0.14\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}+\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+2\mathrm{NH_3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since only $\Delta G^0$ is additive and from $\Delta G^0=-nFE^0$ it follows:

$$
E_{\mathrm{f2}}=2\times(-0.02)-(-0.14)=0.10\ \mathrm{V}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Cu}+2\mathrm{NH_3},
&E_{\mathrm{f1}}&=-0.14\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}+\mathrm{e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}+2\mathrm{NH_3},
&E_{\mathrm{f2}}&=0.10\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $E_{\mathrm{f1}}<E_{\mathrm{f2}}$ the $\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_2]^+}$ ion doesn't disproportionate (the emf would be $-0.14-0.10=-0.24\ \mathrm{V}$).

problems.title: Problem 3 — Organic Synthesis: Synthesis of Haloperidol
problems.statement: Haloperidol is a powerful neuroleptic prescribed in cases of psychomotoric disorder and for the treatment of various psychoses. A synthesis of this compound is proposed.

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement:
Give a scheme for the preparation of methyl 4-chlorobenzoate starting from benzene and all necessary inorganic substances. Diazomethane ($\mathrm{H_2CN_2}$) must be used in your synthesis.

$\gamma$-Butyrolactone (**J**) is a cyclic ester represented below.

![](p3-fig1)
How can $\gamma$-butyrolactone **J** be converted into 4-hydroxybutanoic acid (**K**)?

Convert **K** into 4-chlorobutanoyl chloride (**L**).

The reactions described below do not correspond to those used in the industrial synthesis of haloperidol for which the route is quite complex.

Methyl 4-chlorobenzoate is treated with an excess of vinylmagnesium bromide in anhydrous ether. **M** is obtained after hydrolysis. When **M** is treated with an excess of hydrogen bromide in anhydrous conditions in the presence of benzoyl peroxide, **N** is obtained. **N** reacts with ammonia to form 4-(4-chlorophenyl)-4-hydroxypiperidine (**O**).

Write down the structure of **M**, **N** and **O** and indicate the mechanism of the reaction leading to **M**.

In the presence of a moderate amount of aluminium chloride, **L** reacts with fluoro-benzene to yield mainly a ketone **P** ($\mathrm{C_{10}H_{10}OFCl}$).
Sketch the structure of **P** and indicate the mechanism.

Give a chemical and physical test method for the determination of the carbonyl group. How can you make sure that the carbonyl group does not belong to an aldehyde group?

**P** reacts with **O** in basic media in a $1:1$ molar ratio to give **H** that contains only one chlorine atom on the aromatic ring.
Give the structure of **H** which is haloperidol.
State the multiplicity of each resonance in the $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum of **K**. Assume that all coupling constants between protons and adjacent carbons are identical.

problems.title: Problem 4 — Roasting Zinc Blende
problems.statement:
The production of zinc from zinc blende, $\mathrm{ZnS}$, is a two-stage process: roasting in air and reduction of the zinc oxide formed with carbon monoxide. Consider the roasting reaction:

$$
\mathrm{ZnS(s)+\tfrac32 O_2(g)\longrightarrow ZnO(s)+SO_2(g)},\qquad
\Delta_\mathrm r H^\circ_{1350}=-448.98\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

Industrially, the reaction is carried out at $1350\ \mathrm K$.

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement: Show that the reaction is self-sustaining: the heat evolved is sufficient to bring the reactants from ambient temperature to the reaction temperature. Assume that the mineral contains only $\mathrm{ZnS}$.

Starting with a stoichiometric mixture of one mole of zinc blende and the necessary amount of air at $298\ \mathrm K$, calculate the temperature to which the mixture can be raised by the heat evolved in roasting at $1350\ \mathrm K$, at standard pressure. Is the reaction self-sustaining? The volume ratio of oxygen to nitrogen in air is $1:4$.

Assume that the gangue contains only unreactive silica, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$. Calculate the minimum zinc sulphide content for which roasting remains self-sustaining at $1350\ \mathrm K$. Express the result as grams of $\mathrm{ZnS}$ per $100\ \mathrm g$ of zinc blende.

The standard molar heat capacities are averaged over the temperature range considered.

| Substance | $c_p/(\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}})$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $\mathrm{ZnS}$ (solid) | 58.05 |
| $\mathrm{ZnO}$ (solid) | 51.64 |
| $\mathrm{SO_2}$ (gas) | 51.10 |
| $\mathrm{O_2}$ (gas) | 34.24 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ (gas) | 30.65 |
| $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ (solid) | 72.50 |

Molar masses: $M(\mathrm{ZnS})=97.5\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$; $M(\mathrm{SiO_2})=60.1\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

sections.statement:
Let $n$ be the number of moles of silica per mole of zinc sulphide. The heat required to bring $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{ZnS}$, $n\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, $1.5\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $6\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{N_2}$ from $298$ to $1350\ \mathrm K$ is:

$$
\Delta_\mathrm r H^\circ=
\int_{298}^{1350}\sum_i n_i c_p(i)\,dT
=\int_{298}^{1350}(293.3+72.5n)\,dT.
$$

$$
448980=(293.3+72.5n)(1350-298),\qquad n=1.84\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$
This corresponds to $110.6\ \mathrm g$ of silica per $97.5\ \mathrm g$ of zinc sulphide, or $46.9\ \mathrm g$ of zinc sulphide per $100\ \mathrm g$ of mineral. The minimum content is $46.9\%$.

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The question prints a negative roasting enthalpy; the solution uses $\Delta_\mathrm rH^\circ$ for its positive heat magnitude. The native solution places the maximum-temperature calculation under 4.1 and the silica calculation under 4.2, despite the question's request numbering. Those placements are retained.

problems.title: Problem 5 — Decomposition of Nitramide
problems.statement:
Nitramide, $\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}$, decomposes slowly in aqueous solution to nitrous oxide, $\mathrm{N_2O(g)}$, and water. The experimental rate law is:

$$
\frac{d[\mathrm{N_2O}]}{dt}=k\frac{[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}]}{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}.
$$

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement: What is the apparent order of this reaction in a buffer solution?

Which of the following mechanisms is consistent with the experimental rate law? Justify your choice.

**Mechanism 1**

$$\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}\xrightarrow{k_1}\mathrm{N_2O+H_2O}\qquad\text{slow}$$

**Mechanism 2**

$$\mathrm{NO_2NH_2+H_3O^+}\mathrel{\mathop{\rightleftharpoons}^{k_2}_{k_{-2}}}\mathrm{NO_2NH_3^++H_2O}\qquad\text{rapid}$$

$$\mathrm{NO_2NH_3^+}\xrightarrow{k_3}\mathrm{N_2O+H_3O^+}\qquad\text{slow}$$

**Mechanism 3**

$$\mathrm{NO_2NH_2+H_2O}\mathrel{\mathop{\rightleftharpoons}^{k_4}_{k_{-4}}}\mathrm{NO_2NH_3^-+H_3O^+}\qquad\text{rapid}$$

$$\mathrm{NO_2NH^-}\xrightarrow{k_5}\mathrm{N_2O+OH^-}\qquad\text{slow}$$

$$\mathrm{H_3O^++OH^-}\xrightarrow{k_6}\mathrm{2H_2O}\qquad\text{very fast}$$
Express the observed rate constant $k$ in terms of the rate constants of the elementary steps.

Show that hydroxyl ions catalyse the decomposition.

The reaction is carried out at constant temperature in a buffer solution. The volume of the solution and the volume of the gas space above it are constant. Nitrous oxide is insoluble in water. The following gas pressures are measured:

| $t/\mathrm{min}$ | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $p/\mathrm{Pa}$ | 0 | 6800 | 12400 | 17200 | 20800 | 24000 |

After a long time, the pressure is $40000\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
Derive the relationship between $p$ and $t$, using $k'=k/[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$.
Verify the relationship graphically.
Calculate $k'$ and give its units.

sections.statement:
In a buffer, $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ is constant, so the reaction is first order:

$$v=k'[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}].$$

For the three mechanisms:

$$v_1=k_1[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}],$$

$$v_2=k_3[\mathrm{NO_2NH_3^+}]=\frac{k_3k_2}{k_{-2}}[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}],$$

$$v_3=k_5[\mathrm{NO_2NH^-}]=\frac{k_5k_4}{k_{-4}}\frac{[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}]}{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}.$$

The third mechanism is consistent with the rate law.

Since $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=K_e/[\mathrm{OH^-}]$:

$$v=\frac{k}{K_e}[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}][\mathrm{OH^-}].$$

From $pV=nRT$:

$$d[\mathrm{N_2O}]=\frac{dp(\mathrm{N_2O})}{RT},$$

$$v=\frac{d[\mathrm{N_2O}]}{dt}=\frac1{RT}\frac{dp(\mathrm{N_2O})}{dt}=\frac1{RT}\frac{dp}{dt}=k\frac{[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}]}{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}.$$

The printed material balance is:

$$V[\mathrm{NO_2NH_2}]=n(\mathrm{NO_2NH_2})_\mathrm{init}-n(\mathrm{N_2O})=n(\mathrm{N_2O})_\infty-n(\mathrm{N_2O}).$$

Consequently:

$$\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{k}{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}\frac{RT}{V}\bigl(n_\infty-n\bigr)=\frac{k}{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}(p_\infty-p)=k'(p_\infty-p).$$

Integration gives:

$$p=p_\infty(1-e^{-k't}),\qquad e^{-k't}=1-\frac p{p_\infty}.$$
![](p5-sol-fig1)

The graph of $f(x)=\ln(1-p/p_\infty)=-k't$ is a straight line. The printed key calls its slope $k'$.

$$k'=3.7\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}.$$

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The rapid first step of mechanism 3 prints $\mathrm{NO_2NH_3^-}$, whereas the following slow step and key use $\mathrm{NO_2NH^-}$. Both native forms are retained. The printed claim that the slope is $k'$ is retained alongside its equation $-k't$.

problems.title: Problem 6 — Bio-organic Chemistry
problems.statement:
The dehydrogenation of succinate to fumarate in the Krebs cycle is catalysed by succinic dehydrogenase. Flavine-adenine-dinucleotide, FAD, acts as a coenzyme.

![](p6-fig1)

The stereochemistry of this reaction can be studied with 2,3-dideuteriosuccinates. These compounds may be prepared from related acids or by catalytic deuteration, using palladium on coal, of maleic or fumaric acid.

![](p6-fig2)

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement:
Represent in Fischer projections all stereoisomers obtained by catalytic deuteration of maleic acid and fumaric acid. How many stereoisomers are formed? Which are optically active? What are the relationships between the different stereoisomers? Represent their most stable conformations in Newman projections.

The proportion of dideuterated fumarate formed by the enzymatic dehydrogenation is $4\%$ when the starting dideuteriosuccinate is prepared from fumaric acid and $48.5\%$ when it is prepared from maleic acid. Assume that the molecules adopt their most stable conformation at the enzyme site.
What percentages of dideuterated fumarate would be obtained by a syn or an anti dehydrogenation? Assume that the theoretical percentages are $0\%$ or $50\%$.

Deduce the stereochemistry of the enzymatic dehydrogenation.

Fumarase catalyses the addition of water to fumarate, giving $(S)$-malate, or L-malate.

![](p6-fig3)

When dideuterofumarate reacts, the product is $(2S,3S)$-dideuteromalate. Show schematically the addition of water, using the following representation of the plane containing the fumarate molecule.

![](p6-fig4)

Acetylcoenzyme A, $\mathrm{CH_3COSCoA}$, and glyoxylate react in the presence of malate synthetase to form $(S)$-malate.

![](p6-fig5)

A similar reaction occurs between $\mathrm{CH_3COOR'}$, an analogue of the thioester, and $\mathrm{R''CHO}$, an analogue of glyoxylate, in the presence of $\mathrm{R'O^-}$. It yields the $\beta$-hydroxyester $\mathrm{R''CH(OH)CH_2C(=O)OR'}$. The base produces an intermediate carbanion.

Write the different steps of the mechanism of this reaction.

Acetylcoenzyme A is prepared from acetic acid labelled with deuterium and tritium, $\mathrm{CHDTCOOH}$, with the $(R)$ configuration shown below. $\mathrm T={}^{3}_{1}\mathrm H$ and $\mathrm D={}^{2}_{1}\mathrm H$.

![](p6-fig6)

The $(S)$-malate formed is dehydrated by an enzyme, in the reverse direction of the reaction in 6.4.

What is this enzyme?

The major product is $79\%$ monotritiated fumarate; $21\%$ is untritiated fumarate.
Represent, in Fischer projections, the two possible structures of the major $(S)$-malate formed from the $(R)$-labelled acetylcoenzyme A.
What products would be obtained starting from $(S)$-labelled acetylcoenzyme A?

sections.statement:
There are three isomers. Catalytic deuteration is syn.

![](p6-sol-fig7)

The most stable conformation is the anti conformation, in which the $\mathrm{COO^-}$ groups are at the greatest distance from each other.

![](p6-sol-fig8)

The printed text states: “I and II are enantiomeres, II and III are a meso isomer, thus there are in total three isomers (two enantiomers and one meso form).” Each threo isomer and the meso isomer are diastereomers.

Syn dehydrogenation of I or II gives fumarate without deuterium or with two deuterium atoms, in equal amounts ($50\%$). Anti dehydrogenation gives monodeuterated fumarate. The $4\%$ value indicates anti dehydrogenation.

Syn dehydrogenation of the meso isomer gives only monodeuterated fumarate. Anti dehydrogenation gives $50\%$ normal fumarate and $50\%$ dideuterated fumarate. The experimental $48.5\%$ value from maleic acid is consistent with the meso isomer and anti dehydrogenation.

The enzymatic dehydrogenation is anti, as shown above. The following labelled acetylcoenzyme A reaction is also printed under this solution label:

![](p6-sol-fig9)

![](p6-sol-fig10)

“Stereospecific addition, syn or anti.” Syn addition gives $(2S,3R)$ or $(2R,3S)$.

![](p6-sol-fig11)

Anti addition gives $(2S,3S)$-dideuteromalate.

![](p6-sol-fig12)
![](p6-sol-fig13)
“We would have (2R) (3R) if the enzyme did not produce enantiospecific addition. Thus: enantiospecific addition anti.”

Thus $Y=\mathrm T$ and $X=\mathrm H$ or $\mathrm D$; two projections are printed.

![](p6-sol-fig14)

Starting from the $(S)$ configuration gives inversion at carbon 3 of L-malate. The native diagrams show two major-product projections and one minor-product projection, with $79\%$ nontritiated fumarate and $21\%$ monotritiated fumarate.

![](p6-sol-fig15)

problems.title: Problem 7 — Continuous Hydrogenation of Benzene
problems.statement:
Tick the appropriate boxes in the answer-sheet tables.

Benzene is hydrogenated continuously to cyclohexane:

$$\mathrm{C_6H_6+3H_2}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}\qquad\text{catalyst},\qquad\Delta H^\circ=214\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\text{ at }200\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.$$

Two types of reactor are considered.

**Plug reactor.** The flows $F_1$ and $F_2$ are introduced and mixed at the inlet. A marked slice of the reaction mixture moves through the reactor without mixing with other slices. $F_3$ is the outlet flow. At steady state, the composition is independent of time but depends on position.

![](p7-fig1)

**Stirred reactor.** The flows $F_1$ and $F_2$ are mixed perfectly and instantaneously. At steady state, the composition is independent of time and identical at every point.

![](p7-fig2)

The differential yield is defined by:

$$Y=-\frac{d[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]}{d[\mathrm{C_6H_6}]},\qquad p=\frac{[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]}{[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]+[\mathrm{C_6H_6}]}.$$

Figure 3 shows the differential yield as a function of $p$.

![](p7-fig3)

The aim is to obtain $0.9\le p\le1$ with the best mean yield:

$$Y=-\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]}{\Delta[\mathrm{C_6H_6}]}.$$

sections.title: Questions

parts.statement: For a stirred reactor, determine the value of $p$ giving the maximum mean yield and the maximum value of $Y$.
For a plug reactor with $0.9\le p\le1$, estimate the mean yield: $0.97$, $0.98$, $0.99$ or $1$.
Shade on Figure 3 the losses for a plug reactor (P) and for a combination of a stirred reactor and a plug reactor (MP).
For an annual consumption of $100000$ tons of benzene, calculate the loss with P and with MP.

sections.statement: At steady state, the composition of a stirred reactor is uniform, so the differential yield $y$ equals the mean yield $Y$. The maximum is $y=0.99$ at $p=0.95$. The printed key refers to Figure 1.

For a slice of a plug reactor, at the entry $[\mathrm{C_6H_6}]=1$ and $[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]=0$, so $p=0$ and $y=0.97$. At the outlet, $[\mathrm{C_6H_6}]=0$ and $[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}]=1$, so $p=1$ and $y=0.985$. The mean over $p$ is $0.98$ (Figure 1).

The quantity of benzene lost, not hydrogenated, is $1-p$. The loss for P is shaded in Figure 1. For MP, the loss in the stirred reactor is $1-0.99=0.01$, independent of $p$ up to $0.95$. Above $0.95$, the plug reactor has the same loss as in Figure 1.

![](p7-sol-fig4)

![](p7-sol-fig5)

P: $2\%$ loss, corresponding to $2000$ tons.

MP: the yield is $0.99$, except for $0.95<p<1$, where there is a slight decrease to $0.985$ which is neglected. The overall yield is $0.99$, giving a loss of $1000$ tons.

Native P loss graph, printed in solution Figure 1

The question prints a positive $\Delta H^\circ$ and uses uppercase $Y$ for both differential and mean yield. The key uses lowercase $y$ for differential yield and repeatedly calls its graph Figure 1, whereas the question's yield graph is Figure 3. The sentence “quantity of benzene lost ... $1-p$” is preserved alongside the shaded native yield graphs. The requested blank answer-sheet tables are absent from the obtained collection pages.
